statement: How a death enters a count of drug deaths depends on the country, the register and the period, so figures from different sources do not count the same thing, and studies that matched the same deaths across two sources found that they overlapped only partly. In US national statistics a drug overdose death is one whose underlying cause on the death certificate is coded to ICD-10 X40–X44 (unintentional), X60–X64 (suicide), X85 (assault) or Y10–Y14 (undetermined intent); deaths from long-term drug effects and from side effects of medicines taken as prescribed are left out. A drug counts as involved when the certifier, usually a medical examiner or coroner, wrote it anywhere on the certificate, unless the words around it say otherwise, and a death with several drugs is counted under each of them, so the 15 drug-specific counts for 2023 added up to 179,965 against 106,352 deaths (editors' arithmetic); the National Center for Health Statistics calls its drug counts minimums and says that the certificate cannot show which drug caused a death involving several (Garnett et al., 2026). ICD-10 codes put different drugs together (fentanyl and tramadol share one code; oxycodone, morphine and codeine share another): in Washington State in 2003–2010 one code covered 2,725 poisoning deaths whose certificates named oxycodone, morphine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, codeine or just 'opiate', which only the certificate's words could separate (Ossiander, 2014). The certifier's words also decide whether and how a death is coded: a US consensus panel convened by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration notes that 'acute cocaine intoxication' is coded as a poisoning while 'cocaine use' or 'cocaine abuse' is coded as a mental and behavioural disorder (Goldberger et al., 2013), and 'drug overdose' with no drug named is coded as unspecified drugs (Slavova et al., 2015). The same panel separated deaths caused by a drug from deaths in which a drug was only detected, for example a man shot dead with a drug in his blood, who counts as a drug-detected death but not a drug-caused one (Goldberger et al., 2013). European registers differ again. Norway's Cause of Death Registry, under the European (EMCDDA, now EUDA) definition, counts only the underlying cause and the first contributing cause (Amundsen, 2017). In Sweden, a national selection counted a listed drug code anywhere on the certificate, the European selection only the underlying cause from a shorter list, and a forensic register any death in which an illegal drug, methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl was found at forensic examination, whatever the certified cause (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In England and Wales, the Office for National Statistics counts a death under a specific opioid only when the coroner's conclusion names it (Chen et al., 2025). Who decides differs as well: certifying physicians in Sweden and Norway, coroners in England and Wales, medical examiners or coroners in the US, and, for Norway's second register, local and central police (Fugelstad et al., 2020; Amundsen, 2017; Chen et al., 2025; Garnett et al., 2026). Matching the same deaths across two sources, the strongest evidence on this question, showed partial overlap in three countries. In Norway in 2007–2009, the Cause of Death Registry (822 deaths) and the police registry (562) together covered 929 people, of whom 455 (49%) were in both; 367 were only in the cause-of-death count, 74 police-registry deaths had a certified cause outside the European definition, and 33 had no match (39% of them not Norwegian citizens, the rest with missing or wrong identity numbers). Deaths only in the cause-of-death count were older, more often certified as dependence or suicide, more often had morphine or codeine, methadone or other synthetic opioids rather than heroin as the first drug listed, less often had an autopsy and more often occurred in hospitals or other institutions; autopsies were recorded for 715 of the 822, and the author states that neither source gives the correct figure (Amundsen, 2017). In Sweden in 1994–2012, the certificate-based selection and the forensic toxicology register shared 4,238 of the 9,707 deaths in either, with 2,210 only in the toxicology register and 3,259 only in the certificate selection; among deaths in the toxicology register whose main drug was heroin, 96% were also in the certificate selection, against 23% where it was cannabis (THC). The authors conclude that comparing numbers or rates of drug deaths between countries misleads, while comparing trends is meaningful where investigation and certification have not changed, although they analysed no other country (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, where the state medical investigator examines suspected drug deaths with a full autopsy and toxicology by policy, vital statistics and the medical investigator's records each held 1,046 of the 1,105 residents' poisoning deaths found in either, and 987 were in both. Of 59 deaths counted as poisonings only by vital statistics, 24 occurred in another state, 13 had never been reported to the medical investigator and 15 were natural deaths in the medical investigator's records (such as cirrhosis, sepsis or heart disease) that vital statistics coded as non-dependent drug use because the certificate said 'use' or 'abuse'; of 59 counted only by the medical investigator, 37 had been coded as natural deaths because poisoning was written only in Part II of the certificate, and 17 as other injuries (Landen et al., 2003). Wider local definitions add other deaths: of 70 deaths that a coroner-fed UK register counted as drug-related in Liverpool (deaths in 2004 and inquests in January to June 2005), the register itself placed 21 outside its category for people with a known history of problem drug use, 25 were not deaths from drug toxicity, and 15 were of people living elsewhere (Beynon et al., 2007). Around 2000 in England and Wales, as cited by Webb et al. (2003), coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse numbered 605 (2000), the same register counted 1,296 drug-related deaths (2000) and the Office for National Statistics 2,943 deaths with drug poisoning as the underlying cause (1999). The linkage studies come from Norway, Sweden and one US state, the newest data are from 2012, and none comes from southern Europe. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: How is a death counted as a drug death? It depends on the country and on the list. In the US, a death counts when drug poisoning is the main cause on the death certificate, and every drug written on it is counted, so one death can count under several drugs. Some European lists count only the main cause; one Swedish list counted every death in which a drug was found in tests, whatever the cause. Doctors, coroners, medical examiners or police decide, depending on the place, and the words written on the certificate decide how it is counted. When researchers matched the same deaths on two lists, the lists did not fully agree: in Norway (2007 to 2009) about half of the people were on both lists, in Sweden (1994 to 2012) fewer than half, and in one US state (1995 to 1998) about 9 in 10. So counts from different countries or lists are not the same thing. These matching studies come from three places, and the newest data are from 2012.
population: Deaths counted as drug deaths in national and local registers: United States (national statistics 2017–2023; Washington State 2003–2010; New Mexico residents 1995–1998), Norway 2007–2009, Sweden 1994–2012, England and Wales around 2000, Liverpool 2004–2005
exposure: The definition and source used to count a death as a drug death: ICD-10 underlying-cause and drug codes, drugs named on the death certificate, drugs found in forensic toxicology, police selection or a coroner-fed register's own definition, and who decides
comparator: Other definitions and sources for the same population and period; in the linkage studies, the same deaths matched across two sources
outcome: Which deaths are counted as drug deaths, and how far two sources counting drug deaths in the same place and period agree on the individual deaths
magnitude: Definitions: US overdose deaths, ICD-10 underlying cause X40–X44, X60–X64, X85, Y10–Y14; drugs counted when mentioned in Part I, Part II or the injury description; 2023, 15 drug-specific counts sum to 179,965 for 106,352 deaths (1.69 times; 1.47 times in 2017; editors' arithmetic) (Garnett et al., 2026). Washington State 2003–2010: one code (T40.2) covered 2,725 deaths naming six terms (Ossiander, 2014). Linkage: Norway 2007–2009, 929 people, 455 (49%) in both registers, 367 (40%) cause-of-death register only, 74 (8%) police register with a cause outside the European definition, 33 (4%) unmatched (Amundsen, 2017). Sweden 1994–2012: 4,238 of 9,707 in both the certificate selection and the toxicology register, 2,210 toxicology only, 3,259 certificate only; capture of toxicology-register deaths by the certificate selection, heroin 96%, THC 23% (Fugelstad et al., 2020). New Mexico 1995–1998: 1,046 in each source, 987 in both, 1,105 in either (94.7% and 89.3%); discordant deaths 59 each way (Landen et al., 2003). Liverpool 2004–2005: of 70 register deaths, 21 outside the problem-drug-use category, 25 not from drug toxicity, 15 non-residents (Beynon et al., 2007). England and Wales, as cited: 605 coroners' verdicts (2000), 1,296 register deaths (2000), 2,943 ONS drug-poisoning deaths (1999) (Webb et al., 2003). No intervals; counts of linked records.

evidence.extracted: Norway: physicians must issue death certificates, coded in ICD-10 by the Cause of Death Registry (CDR), and must notify the police of unnatural deaths, including use or suspected use of narcotics; the police decide whether an autopsy is performed, with no obligation when narcotics are suspected. risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded. The overlap counts come from matching complete registers on personal identity numbers (Norway, Sweden) or by hand with a case-by-case review of the discordant deaths (New Mexico) (cards sc_amundsen_2017, sc_fugelstad_2020, sc_landen_2003: JBI moderate, high and moderate). The reporting errors on those cards (a Swedish total printed as 6,648 and 6,448; one-death slips in New Mexico's union columns; a few cells of Norway's Table 1) change the overlaps by a few deaths, not their size, and the high rating of the Swedish card concerns its comparison with the Stockholm inventory, which this claim does not use. The definitions are taken from the bodies that apply them (NCHS, card sc_garnett_2026) or from the papers that describe their own registers.

inconsistency.note: The overlap ranges from about half (Norway: two different selecting bodies and definitions) to about nine in ten (New Mexico: two sources for the same poisoning deaths under similar definitions); the differences follow the definitions compared, as the claim says.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: each figure is given with its place, source and years, and no overlap figure is carried to other countries or to today. The claim states that the linkage data end in 2012 and that none comes from southern Europe.

imprecision.note: Counts of linked records from complete registers; no sampling.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim about how deaths are counted and how far sources agree: starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3). Not downgraded: three independent linkage studies in different countries and systems (Norway, Sweden, New Mexico) agree that sources counting drug deaths in the same place and period disagree on substantial numbers of individual deaths, in both directions, and each traces the disagreement to definitions, certificate wording, residency rules and reporting routes; comparisons of two sources for the same deaths are the strongest evidence on this question. The definitions are taken from the bodies that apply them. The consensus statement (Goldberger et al., 2013) and the Liverpool register study (Beynon et al., 2007) illustrate definitions and add no rate; the England and Wales counts quoted by Webb et al. (2003) come from other sources and different years and are given only as cited. Status replicated: independent studies in three countries point the same way. Whether official counts miss drug deaths, and by how much, is a separate answer.

statement: In the three places studied, official counts built from death certificates or coroners' conclusions named heroin in fewer deaths than a fuller review of the investigation files found (Maryland; Victoria, Australia) or a projection estimated (England and Wales), mainly because morphine (which heroin turns into in the body) or a general term such as mixed drug toxicity was written instead; the fuller reviews used their authors' own definitions, which partly counted heroin markers found in toxicology rather than a judgement that heroin caused the death, and in the one place that looked, a few deaths coded as heroin were judged not to be heroin deaths. In Maryland in 2012–2015, certificates written by the state's medical examiner named heroin in 1,130 overdose deaths, while a protocol built by the state's agencies, which also counted deaths with 6-monoacetylmorphine (a breakdown product of heroin) in toxicology, morphine together with quinine (described as a common heroin additive), or morphine or no named drug on the certificate together with scene evidence of heroin, found 2,182; because the protocol includes every certificate naming heroin, it could only add deaths. Of the 1,052 it added, the certificate named morphine in 804, no specific drug in 193 and another substance in 55. Certificates named heroin in 51.8% (95% CI 49.7 to 53.9) of the protocol's heroin deaths, rising from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, and less often for people aged 55 or older (41.9%), for women (35.1%) and for Black women (25.9%); the authors note that some of the added deaths, including some of the 55, may not have been heroin deaths (Horon et al., 2018). In Victoria, Australia, in 2012–2013, 243 deaths met the authors' own heroin-attribution model applied to closed coroners' files (toxicology together with the circumstances; 6-acetylmorphine was detected in 180, so 63 rested on morphine findings and circumstances), and the national heroin code was missing from 82 of them, leaving the national count 78 lower (165). Of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin, 37 were not coded as heroin, mostly because of the wording (a general cause with the drugs listed only in a database field, morphine written as the cause, or a complication such as brain injury from lack of oxygen written first); 34 of 39 deaths certified as due to morphine or another opioid and all 5 certified as general drug toxicity lacked the heroin code (coders gave it to the other 5 of these 44, although the coroner had not named heroin), and 20 deaths had no code at all. In the other direction, 4 deaths coded as heroin were judged by the model to have involved heroin only by coincidence (Stam et al., 2019). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, the Office for National Statistics counted 13,471 deaths in which the coroner's conclusion named heroin or morphine; in coroner-reported cases of a national programme on drug deaths, 29% (2011) to 36% (2022) of heroin or morphine deaths had an ambiguous cause with the toxicologist implicating the drug, and applying these shares to the national counts, without linking the records, projects about 20,323, about half as many again (editors' calculation); the median number of drugs detected in these deaths rose from four to six (Chen et al., 2025). A scoping review reports, second-hand, similar shifts in US county reviews: in Allegheny County in 2008–2010, heroin deaths rose from 171 to 245 after review while deaths attributed to morphine fell from 132 to 41 and to codeine from 34 to 5, and in New York City in 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication were attributed to heroin (Gutkind et al., 2025). Why heroin is missed, as the authors describe it from the literature: heroin turns quickly into 6-acetylmorphine and then into morphine, so morphine found after death may come from heroin or from morphine itself, and 6-acetylmorphine may not be found after a long interval between use and death or in stored samples (Stam et al., 2019; Horon et al., 2018). US national statistics note that morphine on certificates may reflect heroin, which would understate heroin and overstate morphine (Garnett et al., 2026), and a US medical examiners' position paper treats 6-acetylmorphine as sufficient evidence of heroin and a morphine-to-codeine ratio above 1 as possible evidence, without a cited test of these rules (Davis et al., 2020). None of these studies checked its fuller review against an independent standard, and all concern 2006–2022; whether the deaths added by the reviews were caused by heroin, rather than involving it, is not shown, and what an opioid level after death can show is a separate question. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do official counts miss heroin deaths? In three places studied, official counts named heroin less often than closer checks suggested. Heroin turns into morphine in the body, so morphine is often found after death, and certificates often said morphine or 'mixed drugs' instead of heroin. In Maryland (2012 to 2015), certificates named heroin in about 1,100 deaths, while a fuller check found about 2,200. In Victoria, Australia (2012 to 2013), the official heroin code was missing from 82 of 243 deaths a fuller check linked to heroin, and a few deaths coded as heroin were judged not to be heroin deaths. In England and Wales (2011 to 2022), one estimate made without matching records suggests about half as many again as official counts showed. The fuller checks used their own rules, partly based on heroin traces found in tests, and nobody checked those rules against an independent standard.
population: Overdose deaths investigated by Maryland's statewide medical examiner, 2012–2015; deaths in Victoria, Australia, with closed coroners' files, 2012–2013; deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales, 2011–2022; second-hand, two US county reviews (2006–2010)
exposure: Heroin named in the certificate's cause of death, or the national heroin code (ICD-10 T40.1) built from it, or a coroner's conclusion naming heroin or morphine
comparator: A fuller review of the same files with its own definition (toxicology markers, scene evidence and the coroner's findings), or, in England and Wales, a projection from a coroner-reported register with toxicology
outcome: Deaths meeting the fuller definition of a heroin-related death that the certificate or code did not attribute to heroin, and coded heroin deaths that the fuller review did not count
magnitude: Maryland 2012–2015 (Horon et al., 2018): 1,130 deaths with heroin on the certificate against 2,182 by the enhanced protocol (28.6% and 55.1% of 3,957 overdose deaths, a total not defined in the paper); added 1,052: morphine certified 804, no specific drug 193, other substance 55; certificates named heroin in 51.8% (49.7–53.9) of protocol deaths, 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015); 41.9% at 55 or older, 35.1% of women, 25.9% (18.5–33.3) of Black women. statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the kind of official who investigates a death changes how drug deaths are counted. In the US, counties served by coroners recorded drug deaths less specifically than counties served by medical examiners in the same states, but the one study of states that replaced coroners with medical examiners found no detectable improvement in how specifically poisoning deaths were coded, and across nine states taken together, without allowing for the state, the association ran the other way; no study checked which records were right. In the US, medical examiners are appointed physicians, usually forensic pathologists, while coroners are elected or appointed officials whose qualifications vary widely (Goldberger et al., 2013). In Kentucky, for example, a coroner must be at least 24 years old and meet residence rules, no training in medicine or forensic pathology is required, and new coroners must complete 40 hours of basic training; of 48 coroners who answered a 2016 survey, 47 held another job, 28 as funeral directors (Quesinberry et al., 2019). In the 2018 census of US offices, about 80% were in coroner systems, coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which deaths were tested (64.7%), and offices serving fewer than 25,000 people less often had access to toxicology (75.1%, against 96.4% of offices serving 250,000 or more) (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025). In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine states in 2019–2021, deaths in coroner counties had higher odds of being recorded as of undetermined intent, rather than as an accident or a suicide, than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same state and year (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.27; 1.52 to 1.61 after allowing for county characteristics, recorded investigation steps and the person's age, sex and race); without allowing for the state the odds were lower in coroner counties (0.32; 3.1% against 8.9% recorded as undetermined), which the authors attribute to Maryland, a state with a central medical examiner and many undetermined deaths. An alcohol test was recorded for 58.6% of deaths in coroner counties against 84.5% in medical-examiner counties, while autopsies (about 68% and 67%) and opioid tests (about 80% and 79%) were recorded about equally often (editors' percentages); the type of system was taken from a 2024 listing (Lundberg et al., 2026). A scoping review summarizes, second-hand, three studies that found more certificates naming no drug where coroners certify, one with odds ratios of 1.77 (2014) and 3.87 (2018) for an unclassified overdose death in coroner counties (Gutkind et al., 2025); a commentary quotes an earlier analysis in which 92% of overdose certificates named drugs in states with a central medical examiner, against 62% in states with coroners (Slavova et al., 2015, as cited); and a 2019 review reports that Maryland, a central medical-examiner state, recorded 68% of poisoning deaths as of undetermined intent in 2016, against 1% in Connecticut and Massachusetts (Slavova et al., 2019, as cited). Against this, seven states that switched to a medical examiner system in 1976–1996, compared with seven states that did not, chosen for nearness and similar earlier trends, showed no detectable change in the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code (difference-in-differences −0.02 to −0.03, standard errors 0.04 to 0.06, so falls of up to 10 to 14 percentage points from a share near one half could not be ruled out, editors' calculation), in data that ended in 1998 and included poisonings by substances other than drugs (Zaychik, 2024). See the contested question. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does it matter whether a coroner or a medical examiner investigates? It is not clear. In the US, medical examiners are doctors; coroners are often elected, and in some states need no medical training. In nine US states (2019 to 2021), deaths in coroner areas were more often recorded without saying whether the death was an accident or a suicide than deaths in medical examiner areas of the same state. Other studies found that certificates named no drug more often where coroners work. But seven states that switched to medical examiners showed no clear change in how precisely poisoning deaths were recorded, although that study could not rule out a real improvement, and its data end in 1998. Nobody checked which records were right.
population: Drug poisoning deaths in US counties and states served by coroners or medical examiners: nine states, 2019–2021; seven states that switched systems in 1976–1996 and seven comparison states, 1968–1998; US offices in 2018; Kentucky's elected coroners in 2016
exposure: Death investigation by a coroner (elected or appointed, often without medical training) or a change from a coroner to a medical examiner system
comparator: Death investigation by a medical examiner (an appointed physician) in the same state and year; states that kept coroner or mixed systems
outcome: How specifically drug deaths were recorded: manner recorded as undetermined intent, certificates naming no drug, and non-specific poisoning codes
magnitude: Nine US states 2019–2021, undetermined intent in coroner against medical-examiner counties (Lundberg et al., 2026): within state and year, odds ratio 1.79 (1.43–2.27); adjusted 1.52 (1.20–1.95), 1.61 (1.26–2.06), 1.60 (1.25–2.05); pooled without state, 0.32 (0.29–0.35), 558 of 18,232 (3.1%) against 3,329 of 37,198 (8.9%). Alcohol test recorded 58.6% against 84.5% (editors' percentages). Second-hand: unclassified overdose deaths in coroner counties, odds ratios 1.77 (1.08–2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32–6.46) in 2018 (Gutkind et al., 2025); certificates naming drugs 92% (central medical examiner) against 62% (coroner) (Slavova et al., 2015); undetermined share in 2016, 1% to 68% (Slavova et al., 2019). Seven state switches 1976–1996 (Zaychik, 2024): difference-in-differences in the non-specific share −0.02 (SE 0.04), −0.03 (0.05), −0.02 (0.06); editors' 95% intervals −0.10 to 0.06, −0.13 to 0.07, −0.14 to 0.10. US offices 2018: about 80% in coroner systems; toxicology access 75.1% (small) against 96.4% (large) (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025).

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, which is below the floor: very low. Status contested: credible evidence points both ways, cross-sectional associations against the only before-and-after test and a reversed pooled estimate, so the six-part debate box applies. Counted once: the 92% and 62% figures appear in both reviews by the same first author (Slavova et al., 2015; 2019) and come from one earlier analysis (Warner et al., 2013, not read); the scoping review (Gutkind et al., 2025) is cited only for primary studies not read here, labelled second-hand. The Kentucky survey and the 2018 census describe who investigates and with what testing; they do not compare counts. Whether an autopsy or a drug test changes which deaths count as drug deaths is a separate answer.

debate.question: When a coroner rather than a medical examiner investigates, are drug deaths counted differently or less accurately, and would switching systems change the counts?
debate.evidence_yes: In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine US states in 2019–2021, deaths in coroner counties had higher odds of being recorded as of undetermined intent than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same state and year (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.27), and the estimate stayed between 1.52 and 1.61 after allowing for county size, poverty, unemployment, rurality, recorded autopsy and toxicology, suicide notes, investigator narratives and the person's age, sex and race; alcohol tests were recorded less often in coroner counties (58.6% against 84.5%) (Lundberg et al., 2026). A scoping review summarizes three studies that found more certificates naming no drug where coroners certify, one with odds ratios of 1.77 (2014) and 3.87 (2018), with unclassified deaths falling faster in medical-examiner counties (72% against 43%, 2014–2018) and lower odds where the certifier is a pathologist, coroners must be trained or the system is centralized (Gutkind et al., 2025, second-hand). An earlier analysis quoted in a commentary found that 92% of overdose certificates named drugs in states with a central medical examiner, against 62% in coroner states (Slavova et al., 2015, as cited). Coroners in some states need no medical training (Kentucky; Quesinberry et al., 2019), and in 2018 about 80% of US offices were in coroner systems, coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which deaths were tested, and small offices less often had access to toxicology (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025).
debate.evidence_no: The only before-and-after test found no detectable improvement: in seven US states that replaced coroners or justices of the peace with medical examiners in 1976–1996, compared with seven comparison states that did not, the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code did not fall detectably more after the switch (difference-in-differences −0.02 to −0.03) (Zaychik, 2024). Across the nine states taken together, without allowing for the state, deaths in coroner counties were less often recorded as undetermined (3.1% against 8.9%; odds ratio 0.32), which the authors attribute to Maryland, a central medical-examiner state (Lundberg et al., 2026); Maryland recorded 68% of poisoning deaths as undetermined in 2016, against 1% in Connecticut and Massachusetts (Slavova et al., 2019, as cited), so a medical-examiner system can record drug deaths very unspecifically. In the nine-state data, autopsies and opioid tests were recorded about as often in coroner as in medical-examiner counties (editors' percentages; Lundberg et al., 2026).
debate.neither_can_show: No study checked, against an independent review of the same deaths, which recorded intent or drug was correct, so 'undetermined' or 'no drug named' measures how specifically deaths were recorded, not how many were missed or wrongly attributed. Comparisons between counties cannot separate the type of office from what usually comes with it (budget, staff, caseload, access to toxicology, rurality, state law), some of which is part of what a system is; the nine-state study took each county's system from a 2024 listing for deaths in 2019–2021 and combined two surveillance systems by manner of death. The before-and-after study had seven switches, all before 1999, used underlying-cause codes that mix drug and non-drug poisonings, did not allow for repeated years of the same state, and was too imprecise to rule out falls of 10 to 14 percentage points. The 92% and 62% figures and the county odds ratios are second-hand and unadjusted or not appraised here.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the US studies read, deaths investigated in coroner-served areas tended to be recorded less specifically, with no drug named more often and, within states, more often as of undetermined intent, than deaths investigated by medical examiners. Whether that is caused by the type of office, or by the smaller budgets, scarcer testing and officials without medical training that often come with it, is not known, and the only test of a change of system, with data before 1999, could neither show nor rule out an improvement. Maryland shows that a central medical-examiner system can also record many drug deaths as undetermined, so rules and practice within a state matter as well as the title of the office. None of this shows how many drug deaths either system misses or wrongly counts.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Before-and-after studies of recent changes of system or of rules (such as toxicology mandates or certifier training) in the ICD-10 era, with drug-specific outcomes (the share of certificates naming each drug and the share recorded as undetermined), matched comparison areas, enough cases and standard errors that allow for repeated years of the same area; and linkage of certificates in both kinds of system with an independent review of the same deaths, blinded to the type of office, recording each office's budget, staffing and testing, to measure missed and wrongly attributed deaths in both directions.
